01 · The idea

Parts 1 and 2 installed tools. Part 3 plugs things in.

Parts 1 and 2 were eight tools that run on your machine. Part 3 is about connections: things you plug into Claude so it can design motion, generate shots, see a reference and read the numbers, all from the same chat.

The reel is one object: a power strip called Claude Code, at 0/4. Each tool drops in on its cable, the counter goes up, and its card turns into a demo of the job. At 4/4, the comments ask for the setup.

02 · The setup

All four, ready to plug in.

This is what you asked for in the comments. Each block connects one tool and tries it once. Or paste the setup prompt into Claude Code and let it walk you through all four.

01 · hyperframes
# 1 · HyperFrames · motion graphics from a web page (Apache-2.0 · github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes)
# Needs Node 22+ and FFmpeg. Free and open source.
npx hyperframes init my-reel          # new project (it also offers its Claude Code skills)
cd my-reel
npx hyperframes check                 # checks the composition and tells you how to fix each issue
npx hyperframes preview               # live preview in your browser
npx hyperframes render --output reel.mp4
# Then just ask Claude: "animate the title, time the captions to the voice, render 1080x1920".
02 · higgsfield mcp
# 2 · Higgsfield MCP · AI video shots without leaving the chat (paid · uses Higgsfield credits)
# In Claude: Settings -> Connectors -> Add custom connector -> paste the MCP link from Higgsfield's site.
# Sign in to Higgsfield when Claude asks. Then, in any chat:
"Make me a 5-second vertical shot of my product (photo attached): slow orbit,
 soft studio light, no text. Use Seedance. Show me the prompt and the cost before you run it."
# Our rule: every paid generation gets its own OK, and the prompt is always written in full.

Why these two together: HyperFrames builds the motion layer (titles, captions, charts) in code; Higgsfield gives you the shots you can't film. One reel, both layers, one chat.

03 · claude in chrome
# 3 · Claude in Chrome · eyes on any reel (Claude's browser extension)
# Install "Claude in Chrome" from the Chrome Web Store and sign in with your Claude account.
# Then ask Claude (Claude Code or the Claude app) to use your browser:
"Open this reel: <link>. Pause it every 0.5 s, take a screenshot of each frame,
 and give me a table: time, what's on screen, text and size, colour, camera move, cut."
# Tip: if you can download the MP4, frames from FFmpeg are faster and include the audio:
ffmpeg -i reel.mp4 -vf "fps=4,scale=180:-1,tile=10x5" sheet_%02d.jpg
04 · vidiq
# 4 · vidIQ · the numbers behind any account (connector · uses vidIQ credits)
# In Claude: Settings -> Connectors -> add vidIQ and sign in to your vidIQ account.
# Then:
"List the last 40 reels of @account with views, likes and comments.
 Mark the ones with 5x the account's median. For each one: the hook (first 3 s),
 the format, and what we could make from it for our own channel."
# When credits run out, the same list can be read from the public profile in the browser (plug 3).

Why these two together: vidIQ tells you which reel exploded; Claude in Chrome opens it and takes it apart frame by frame. First the numbers, then the eyes.

setup prompt · claude code
You are setting up my editing kit for Claude. Help me plug in these four, one at a time,
and tell me in one line when each one works:
1. HyperFrames: run npx hyperframes init test-reel, then render a 5-second title card to test.mp4.
2. Higgsfield MCP: check that the connector is listed; show me a 5-second shot prompt and its cost, but DON'T run it until I say so.
3. Claude in Chrome: open https://www.instagram.com in my browser and take one screenshot.
4. vidIQ: show me my credit balance, then the 5 most-viewed reels of one account I choose.
If something fails, read the error, fix the cause (Node version, missing FFmpeg, connector not signed in), and retry.
Check 01

Paid runs need an OK.

Higgsfield and vidIQ spend credits. Ask Claude to show the prompt and the cost first, then say go.

Check 02

Model, don't copy.

Study a reference for its structure and pacing. The topic, the props and the look are yours.

Check 03

One test first.

Use all four once in a 10-second test before a real reel. Fixing the setup later costs more.

03 · References

One object, four plugs.

The structure follows a format that works on this kind of reel: a power strip with an empty counter, one plug per tool that drops in on its cable, and a card per tool that turns into its demo. We rebuilt it in our colours, with our tools and our character.

A demo per plug

A mini editor that writes the HTML and renders reel.mp4, a chat that makes a 5-second product shot, a browser with an eye that pauses and screenshots a reel, and a grid of reels where one count rockets to 1.7M.

The power strip

Always on screen, always alive: the counter goes 0/4 → 4/4, the cables stay plugged and swing, and the camera pulls back to it between tools.

Each plug brings its colour

When a plug slams in, its brand colour floods the frame from the socket. Inside each tool the background flips between dark and colour every 3 seconds or so, with soft shapes drifting behind, and every card carries the tool's real logo.

Catalina, as in Parts 1 and 2

Her real poses in the bottom-right corner, changing on the beats, and her face as the user in the chat and in the comments.

04 · Claude session

How this reel was made.

What came back: the reference studied at 4 frames per second, a script written sentence by sentence on its structure, the narration with 146 time-stamped words, and a block-by-block brief for the builder.

The review that changed it: the first cut zoomed hard into every word and cropped the cards at the edges. The camera was calmed down (soft moves, every card always whole) and the energy moved into the content: things typing, counting and plugging in.

What came back: 49 seconds at 1080×1920 and 30 fps, the voice plus sound effects on real events (plugs, clicks, typing, the shutter).

05 · The cut

Six blocks, four plugs.

0:00–0:04

At 0/4.

Don't start editing with Claude Code until you've plugged in these four.
0:04–0:16

A motion designer.

The first is HyperFrames, which turns Claude into a motion designer, so it can write a web page, animate your titles, time your captions and render a real MP4, without you ever opening After Effects.
0:16–0:26

Shots in the chat.

The second is the Higgsfield MCP. Just say, make me a five-second shot of my product, and Claude generates it with Seedance or Kling, without leaving the chat.
0:26–0:35

Eyes on any reel.

The third is Claude in Chrome, which gives Claude eyes on any reel. So you paste a link, and it pauses, screenshots and studies it frame by frame.
0:35–0:45

No more blindfold.

And the last one is vidIQ. It reads the numbers of any account, so Claude finds which reels exploded and which hooks they used, instead of editing blindfolded.
0:45–0:49

Comment PLUG.

If you want to try all four, comment PLUG and we'll send you the setup.
06 · Decisions

Where the taste is.

01

Model a winner

The structure comes from a reel format that already worked. What changes is the topic: editing instead of coding.

02

Show the job, not the logo

No tool logos: each one is a simple mark, and the card shows the tool doing its job.

03

Calm camera

The camera only pulls back between tools. Inside a tool, the content moves, not the frame.

04

Say what costs

Two of the four are paid. The page says so, and the setup never runs a paid generation without an OK.
